overview: The map’s “Ibadites” label covers part of the central Maghreb in 1200 to 1279. It represents a religious and regional grouping, not the lifetime of one empire. The M’Zab oasis towns provide a concrete focus, while clearly dated later examples show communities adapting through colonial rule and beyond.

periods.title: Early oasis towns
periods.summary: The earliest towns in the five-town M’Zab ensemble developed during the eleventh century.

periods.title: The imported map window
periods.summary: Oasis settlement joined houses, religious institutions, palm groves and water management.

periods.title: French colonial rule
periods.summary: French occupation changed institutions and power; Algeria became independent in 1962.

periods.title: Documenting living practices
periods.summary: Researchers interviewed residents about toilets, water and cultivation.

items.text: M’Zab’s fortified towns gather houses around a mosque whose minaret also served as a lookout. The mosque complex could hold grain and defensive supplies. Worship, shared reserves and protection therefore belonged to the same town center.

The compact houses form rings around that center. UNESCO describes a repeated basic house form that protects family privacy while fitting closely beside neighboring homes. The architecture makes room for both a household’s own space and life in a dense community.

In the water system described by architect Said Madani in 2022, paths between gardens become channels during floods. Openings admit water according to factors such as plot size, distance and palm trees. A walkway could have a second job when the water arrived.

During field visits from 2006 to 2018, Boualem Remini studied Ghardaia’s floodwater capture. The muddy water carried fine particles useful to garden soils. Some also soaked underground or entered recharge wells, helping replenish a shallow water reserve after the flood had passed.

Ghardaia’s underground galleries have air shafts, and their entrances can be shut when irrigation is complete or flooding threatens the palm grove. Remini describes earlier sliding stone closures and modern steel ones. Maintaining these moving parts mattered as much as digging the channels in the first place.

Madani describes water controllers using mirrors or fire signals to communicate between diversion points. Their work combines knowledge of the weather with coordination on the ground. Good water sharing depends on people sending the right message, not just on a clever canal.

A study based on 2019 interviews records both family dry toilets and shared facilities in Beni Isguen’s palm grove. These saved scarce water and collected material that residents used as fertilizer. The study documents a remembered and surviving practice, rather than an excavated toilet from 1200.

The same researchers found that deep groundwater extraction and running water encouraged flush toilets during the twentieth century. Wastewater then created new problems where adequate sewerage was missing. Comfort at home and care for an oasis had to be worked out together.

During the colonial period, Ibadi scholars traveled and exchanged ideas between M’Zab, Algiers, Tunis and Cairo. Jomier’s research traces reform debates from the 1920s to the 1950s. An oasis could be geographically remote while its readers remained connected to large cities.

sections.title: Books, learning and a later written sample

items.text: Ibadi book collections can be as small as a few volumes in a family home or as large as an organized private library. Historian Paul Love’s work on North African collections records both surviving family libraries and books dispersed abroad. Preserving learning has often been household work.

A later Arabic example from the wider North African Ibadi tradition begins “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God”. Love transcribes it from folio 1b of Naples manuscript ARA 50, copied in 1762. The book came from Libya, so this is not evidence for a particular M’Zab classroom in 1200.

That manuscript leaves space for diagonal commentary around its main text. It also repeats the last word of one page at the beginning of the next, a device for keeping the sequence straight. Readers and copyists gave the book practical tools for study and navigation.

ending.text: The label’s 1279 endpoint is a map cutoff, not the disappearance of Ibadi communities. France occupied M’Zab in 1882; Algeria became independent in 1962. These political changes transformed local life while the community continued.
